title: Attention, 2014, then the transformer, 2017
story:
The architecture being replaced worked like this: read the whole source sentence, compress it into a single fixed-length vector, then generate the output from that vector alone. Everything the decoder could ever need had to fit in one representation whose size did not depend on the length of the input.

Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio proposed the fix in 2014, and the sentence they used is worth quoting exactly, because it is more careful than the way it is usually repeated. They write that in this paper, we conjecture that the use of a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck in improving the performance of this basic encoder-decoder architecture, and propose to extend this by allowing a model to automatically soft-search for parts of a source sentence that are relevant to predicting a target word, without having to form these parts as a hard segment explicitly.

Conjecture. Not demonstration. The claim that the fixed-length vector is what limits the architecture was a hypothesis about a cause, advanced with a proposed remedy attached — which is the normal and honest shape of a research claim, and it is routinely reported as though the diagnosis had been established first.

It did have support. Cho and colleagues had already shown that the performance of the basic encoder-decoder deteriorated rapidly as input sentence length increased, with sharp degradation beyond twenty to thirty tokens. That is evidence that something goes wrong with length; the conjecture is about what.

Then in 2017 Vaswani and seven co-authors published Attention Is All You Need, which took the mechanism and removed everything around it. If attention can relate any position to any other position directly, the sequential processing is not doing necessary work — and sequential processing was the thing preventing the whole sequence from being handled at once. Dropping it is what made the parallel hardware usable, which is the practical reason the architecture took over.

The formula is worth stating precisely, and so is the reason for its odd-looking scaling factor. Attention takes queries, keys and values; it computes the compatibility of each query with each key, divides by the square root of the key dimension, normalises, and uses the result to weight the values.

That division is where the second conjecture lives, and the paper is explicit about its status. Their observation is that for small key dimensions the two attention mechanisms perform similarly, while additive attention outperforms unscaled dot product attention for larger ones. Their explanation: they suspect that for large values of the key dimension, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients, and that to counteract this effect they scale the dot products. The support is a variance calculation in a footnote — if the components of the queries and keys are independent random variables with mean zero and variance one, their dot product has mean zero and variance equal to the key dimension, so dividing by the square root of that returns the variance to one.

We suspect. Both of the papers that define this lineage hedge their central causal claim, and in both cases the hedge disappeared on the way into textbooks and interview answers, where it is stated that the scaling is required because the dot products saturate the softmax. The empirical result is not in doubt — the fix works, and every major architecture since has kept it. What was never established is that the diagnosed cause is the real one, and later work has noted that dimension is not the only reason dot products might get large.

Keep both the result and its status, because a curriculum about checking claims should not be the place the hedge goes missing. The cost, at least, is not conjectural: relating every position to every other position is quadratic in sequence length, so the fixed-size bottleneck was traded for a cost that grows with the square of the context — which is why most subsequent work on long contexts is an attack on that exponent.

problem.name: Attention over a bottleneck
problem.shape: An output must be produced from a sequence whose relevant parts vary per output step.
tell: performance falls off as inputs get longer

processing is sequential and the hardware is idle

problem.move: Let every output position weight every input position directly rather than reading from a fixed summary, and scale the compatibility scores by the square root of the key dimension. Then keep track of which parts of the justification are measured and which are conjectured, because the two are reported identically.
problem.invariant: Compressing a variable-length input into a fixed-size representation bounds what can be recovered from it regardless of the input's length. Attending directly removes that bound and replaces it with a cost quadratic in length.
problem.breaks: Both foundational papers hedge their central causal claim — a conjecture about the fixed-length bottleneck, a suspicion about softmax gradients — and both hedges vanished in retelling. The remedies are well established empirically; the diagnoses are not, and later work has noted that dimension is not the only reason dot products grow large.

cost.time: relating every position to every other is quadratic in sequence length, which is the binding constraint on context and the target of most subsequent work
cost.space: the pairwise scores and the cached keys and values for every position, which is what makes long contexts expensive to serve as well as to train
cost.beats: the fixed-size summary, which is linear and loses information in a way that worsens with length, and recurrence, which is memory-efficient and cannot be parallelised across the sequence

worked.reasoning:
Attention takes queries, keys and values. It computes the compatibility of each query with each key as a dot product, divides those scores by the square root of the key dimension, normalises them with a softmax, and uses the result to take a weighted combination of the values.

The scaling factor is where the interesting part is, and I would answer it in two halves, because the usual answer gives only the first.

The measured half: the paper reports that for small key dimensions the additive and dot-product mechanisms perform similarly, while additive attention outperforms unscaled dot-product attention for larger ones. That is an observation, and it is what motivates doing something.

The conjectured half: the authors write that they suspect that for large values of the key dimension, the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients, and that to counteract this effect they scale the dot products. The supporting argument is a variance calculation in a footnote — if the components of the queries and keys are independent random variables with mean zero and variance one, their dot product has mean zero and variance equal to the key dimension, so dividing by the square root of the dimension restores unit variance.

Note the word suspect. That is a hypothesis about the mechanism, with an arithmetic argument for plausibility, not a demonstration that saturation is what was actually happening. The correction is worth making because the flattened version — 'the scaling is required because the dot products saturate the softmax' — is stated everywhere as settled, and later work has pointed out that dimension is not the only reason dot products might grow large.

The same pattern appears one paper earlier, which is why I would mention it. Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio introduce attention by writing that they conjecture that the use of a fixed-length vector is a bottleneck in improving the performance of the basic encoder-decoder architecture. Also a conjecture. It had support — the basic encoder-decoder had been shown to deteriorate rapidly with input length, degrading sharply beyond twenty to thirty tokens — but that is evidence that something goes wrong with length, not that the fixed-length vector is the thing that goes wrong.

So both papers that define this lineage hedge their central causal claim, and both hedges disappeared in retelling. That is not a reason to doubt the techniques: the fixes work, every major architecture since has kept them, and the empirical case is overwhelming. It is a reason to be precise about what is established, which is the remedy, versus what is proposed, which is the diagnosis.

The part that is not conjectural is the cost. Relating every position to every other position is quadratic in sequence length, so what was gained was the removal of a fixed-size bottleneck and what was paid was a cost growing with the square of the context — which is why so much subsequent work is an attack on that exponent rather than on the mechanism.

problem.practice: Open both papers and find the words conjecture and suspect. Then compare what they say to the explanation you were taught, and note which parts of the causal story were never actually claimed by the people who proposed the fix.

beats.broke: A variable-length input was compressed into one fixed-size vector before any of it could be used, so what the decoder could recover was bounded regardless of how long the input was.
beats.fix: Let each output position weight every input position directly, then remove the recurrence entirely — which is what made the whole sequence processable at once and the parallel hardware usable.
beats.cost: Relating every position to every other is quadratic in sequence length, so a fixed-size bottleneck was traded for a cost growing with the square of the context.

interview.q: Give the scaled dot-product attention formula and explain what the scaling factor is justified by.
interview.trap: Stating that the scaling is required because large dot products saturate the softmax. The paper says it suspects that, offering a variance argument in a footnote — the empirical motivation is measured, the mechanism is conjectured, and the hedge is usually dropped.
interview.answer:
Attention takes queries, keys and values: compute each query's dot product with each key, divide by the square root of the key dimension, normalise with a softmax, and weight the values by the result.

The scaling factor has two halves and the usual answer gives only one.

Measured: the paper reports that for small key dimensions the additive and dot-product mechanisms perform similarly, while additive attention outperforms unscaled dot-product attention for larger ones. That is the observation motivating any fix.

Conjectured: the authors write that they suspect that for large values of the key dimension the dot products grow large in magnitude, pushing the softmax into regions where it has extremely small gradients, and that they scale to counteract this. The support is a footnote variance argument — with query and key components independent, mean zero, variance one, the dot product has mean zero and variance equal to the dimension, so dividing by its square root restores unit variance.

Note 'suspect'. That is a hypothesis about mechanism with an arithmetic plausibility argument, not a demonstration that saturation was what happened — and the flattened version is stated everywhere as settled, while later work has pointed out that dimension is not the only reason dot products grow large.

The same pattern appears a paper earlier: Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio introduce attention by writing that they conjecture the fixed-length vector is a bottleneck. It had support — the basic encoder-decoder was shown to deteriorate rapidly with length, degrading sharply beyond twenty to thirty tokens — but that is evidence that something goes wrong with length, not that the fixed-length vector is the thing going wrong.

So both defining papers hedge their central causal claim and both hedges vanished in retelling. That is not a reason to doubt the techniques; the fixes work and every architecture since has kept them. It is a reason to be precise about what is established — the remedy — versus what was proposed — the diagnosis.

What is not conjectural is the cost: relating every position to every other is quadratic in sequence length, which is why most later work on long contexts attacks that exponent rather than the mechanism.
